playground.label: Files: Mad Libs with a text file and a replacement function (uses input)
playground.code:
import re, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    source = Path(folder) / 'panda.txt'
    source.write_text('The ADJECTIVE panda walked to the NOUN and then VERB. A nearby NOUN was\nunaffected by these events.', encoding='utf-8')
    text = source.read_text(encoding='utf-8')
    def ask(match):
        word = match.group(1)
        return input('Enter ' + ('an ' if word[0] in 'AEIOU' else 'a ') + word.lower() + ': ')
    result = re.sub(r'\b(ADJECTIVE|NOUN|ADVERB|VERB)\b', ask, text)
    target = Path(folder) / 'panda_filled.txt'
    target.write_text(result, encoding='utf-8')
    print(result)
    print(target.name, target.stat().st_size, target.read_text(encoding='utf-8') == result)

findings: Chapter 10 of the 3rd edition, Reading and Writing Files, teaches filepaths with the pathlib module (Path(), joining with the / operator, the current working directory, the home directory, absolute and relative paths, creating folders, the parts of a path, file sizes and timestamps with stat(), glob patterns and the checks exists(), is_file() and is_dir()); then the reading and writing process for plain text files (read_text() and write_text(), open() with the modes r, w and a and the encoding argument, read(), readlines(), write(), close() and the with statement); saving variables with the shelve module; Project 4, the random quiz generator; and closes with 11 practice questions and 2 practice programs, Mad Libs and Regex Search.

The chapter's printed interactive sessions reproduce under Python 3.14.4 with differences that come from the operating system or the version: its path objects print as WindowsPath because it was run on Windows, and on this Linux machine Path() gives a PosixPath, while the Windows outputs (the str with backslashes, the anchor, the drive, the parts and the parents) are reproduced with PureWindowsPath, whose repr names PureWindowsPath in place of WindowsPath; the TypeError for two strings and the return values 13, 14 and 25 of write_text() and write() are identical; the FileNotFoundError text is printed by the chapter with [WinError 2] and reads [Errno 2] No such file or directory here; and glob(), which the chapter prints as a generator object, gives a map object under 3.14.4 that is single-use in the same way.

Project 4 does not produce the output the chapter prints: run as listed, the program writes 'Capital of West Virginia:' where the chapter shows 'What is the capital of West Virginia?', writes '(Form1)' where it shows '(Form 1)', and writes the answer key as one unbroken line such as 1.D2.C3.C4.B where it shows one answer per line such as '1. D'; in the listing of step 1 as printed the key 'West Virginia' is split over two lines, which is a SyntaxError if typed as shown; the program is otherwise correct, since 35 quizzes of 50 questions with four distinct options each and a key that names the right capital were produced and checked.

The chapter tells the reader to pass encoding='utf-8' because Windows uses cp1252 by default, and the documentation confirms the principle: the default of open() is the encoding of the machine's locale, so UTF-8 text with non-English letters can be read wrongly; it recommends writing the encoding out, offers the opt-in EncodingWarning of PEP 597 (-X warn_default_encoding) to find the places where it was left out, and records that Python 3.15 will make UTF-8 mode the default (PEP 686), which is not yet so in 3.14.4.

The chapter's account of shelve holds in its interface and differs in what lies beneath: a shelf is opened, used like a dictionary and closed, but the files it makes depend on the dbm backend, the chapter lists three files on Windows, one file mydata.db on macOS and one file mydata on Linux, and under 3.14.4 a new shelf uses dbm.sqlite3 and made the single file named in the call on this Linux machine, while dbm.dumb makes the three files .bak, .dat and .dir; the chapter does not warn that the values of a shelf are pickled, which the documentation says makes loading a shelf from an untrusted source insecure, that a changed list inside a shelf is lost unless it is assigned back or writeback=True is used, or that JSON is the usual choice for plain data that is shared.

The chapter's advice on the with statement and on closing holds and is supported by the tutorial and the reference: the with statement calls __exit__ however the block is left, so the file is closed after a normal end, a return or an exception, and the tutorial adds that a write without close() or with may not be completely written to the disk, which the executed run showed for a small write that another reader saw as empty until the close.

For an advanced course, chapter 10 is best taught by asking of each operation whether it only computes a path, asks the file system a question, or changes a file or folder: Path(), the / operator, name, stem, parent and with_suffix() only compute; exists(), is_file(), stat() and glob() ask; write_text(), open() in mode w, a or x, mkdir() and shelve change; the chapter's printed outputs hold under 3.14.4 except the Windows path types, the operating-system text of an error and the generator object of glob(), and encoding and line-ending control, closing, the dbm backend and the pickle warning of a shelf, JSON as the plain alternative and the faults of Project 4's printed output are what the chapter leaves for the course to add.

Current pathlib offers more than the chapter presents: iterdir(), rglob() and the ** pattern, Path.walk() since Python 3.12, mkdir(exist_ok=True), with_suffix(), with_name() and relative_to(), Path.open(), a case_sensitive argument of glob() since 3.12, a full pattern language with [seq] and ** documented for glob(), and in Python 3.14 the methods exists(), is_file() and is_dir() return False instead of raising any OSError; st_ctime is deprecated on Windows since 3.12 in favour of st_birthtime, and PEP 519 lets path objects be passed to open(), os and shelve.

Modern practice warns of traps the chapter leaves out: write_text() and write() return the number of characters, not bytes; text mode translates line endings unless newline is given; a file read to its end returns an empty string until seek(0); the iterator of glob() is used up by one pass and lists paths in no particular order; the mode 'w' empties an existing file at once and the mode 'x' refuses to; the path of a string such as spam\eggs is two names on Windows and one on Linux; a path with .. in it stays as written until resolve() is called; and the drive attribute that the chapter says macOS and Linux paths lack exists there and is the empty string.
title: Reading and writing files for an advanced course: chapter 10 of the 3rd edition and today's Python

nodes.label: Filepaths
nodes.body: Filepaths, the names that say where a file lies, are the base of Chapter 10 (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Path objects
nodes.body: The chapter builds paths with the Path() function of the pathlib module, joins them with the / operator and explains the separators of the operating systems (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Path construction
nodes.body: Path('spam', 'bacon', 'eggs') joins the names with the separator of the operating system: the chapter, run on Windows, prints WindowsPath('spam/bacon/eggs') and str() of it as 'spam\\bacon\\eggs', and on macOS or Linux a PosixPath and 'spam/bacon/eggs' (Sweigart, 2025); on the Linux machine of this study the type of Path('spam', 'bacon', 'eggs') was PosixPath, and the Windows outputs were reproduced with PureWindowsPath, which gives PureWindowsPath('spam/bacon/eggs') and 'spam\\bacon\\eggs', the POSIX class giving 'spam/bacon/eggs'; the chapter says in one sentence that Path() returns a string and in the next that it returns a WindowsPath object, and it is the object that is returned (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Path() joins the names it is given with the separator of the operating system and returns a path object, a PosixPath on macOS and Linux and a WindowsPath on Windows; str() of it gives the path as text.

io.code: (repr(__import__('pathlib').PureWindowsPath('spam', 'bacon', 'eggs').parents[1]), str(__import__('pathlib').PureWindowsPath('spam', 'bacon', 'eggs')))

nodes.label: Path joining
nodes.body: Path('spam') / 'bacon' / 'eggs' gives the same path as Path('spam') / Path('bacon/eggs') and Path('spam') / Path('bacon', 'eggs'), and 'spam' / 'bacon' raises TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for /: 'str' and 'str', because one of the first two operands must be a path; the / operator replaces os.path.join() (Sweigart, 2025); 'spam' / Path('bacon') also works, Path('spam').joinpath('bacon', 'eggs') is the same join as a method, and a right operand that is absolute replaces what lies to its left, Path('spam') / '/etc' being PosixPath('/etc') and os.path.join('spam', '/etc') being '/etc' (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The / operator joins a path object with a string or another path into a new path; one of the first two operands must be a path, because two strings raise TypeError, and os.path.join() is the older function that joins strings.

io.code: ((__import__('pathlib').PurePosixPath('spam') / 'bacon' / 'eggs').parts[:2], repr('spam' / __import__('pathlib').PurePosixPath('bacon')))

nodes.label: Path flavours
nodes.body: On Windows the backslash separates folders and is not allowed in a filename, and on macOS and Linux it is an ordinary character, so the chapter advises forward slashes in source code, which pathlib turns into the right separator; the loop over accounts.txt, details.csv and invite.docx with Path(r'C:\Users\Al', filename) prints C:\Users\Al\accounts.txt and the two like lines (Sweigart, 2025); run here, PureWindowsPath(r'spam\eggs').parts was ('spam', 'eggs') and PurePosixPath(r'spam\eggs').parts was ('spam\\eggs',), one name (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Windows writes paths with backslashes and macOS and Linux with forward slashes, so the same text is two names on Windows and one name on the others; the pure path classes build either kind on any machine without using a disk, and forward slashes in source code work everywhere.

io.code: (__import__('pathlib').PureWindowsPath(r'spam\eggs').parts[:2], __import__('pathlib').PurePosixPath(r'spam\eggs').parts[:2])

nodes.label: Working locations
nodes.body: Where a program is running and where the user keeps files decide how a path is read (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Working directory
nodes.body: Every program has a current working directory, and a name that does not begin at the root folder is read from it; Path.cwd() returns it as a path object, os.getcwd() as a string, and os.chdir() changes it, there being no pathlib function for that, and os.chdir() to a missing folder raises FileNotFoundError (Sweigart, 2025); run here, Path.cwd().name was 'walnut' after os.chdir('delicious/walnut'), the error read [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'ThisFolderDoesNotExist' where the chapter prints the Windows text [WinError 2] The system cannot find the file specified, and hasattr(Path, 'chdir') was False (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Every running program has a current working directory that every path not starting at the root is read from; Path.cwd() and os.getcwd() read it, only os.chdir() changes it, and a folder that does not exist raises FileNotFoundError.

io.code: (__import__('pathlib').Path.cwd().is_absolute(), __import__('os').getcwd() == str(__import__('pathlib').Path.cwd()))

nodes.label: Home directory
nodes.body: Path.home() returns the home folder of the user, C:\Users\Al in the chapter's example, under C:\Users on Windows, /Users on macOS and often /home on Linux (Sweigart, 2025); run here the result was absolute and equal to Path(os.path.expanduser('~')) and to Path('~').expanduser(), and the documentation says a RuntimeError is raised if the home directory cannot be resolved (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Path.home() returns the user's home folder as an absolute path object; where it lies depends on the operating system, and a program can normally read and write files there.

io.code: __import__('pathlib').Path.home().is_absolute()

nodes.label: Absolute versus relative
nodes.body: An absolute path begins with the root folder, C:\ on Windows and / on macOS and Linux, and a relative path is relative to the current working directory; Path.cwd().is_absolute() is True and Path('spam/bacon/eggs').is_absolute() is False, Path.cwd() / Path('my/relative/path') and Path('my/relative/path').absolute() give the same absolute path, and the same relative path can be put after Path.home() instead (Sweigart, 2025); run here absolute() was equal to Path.cwd() / r, and it leaves .. in place, Path('docs/../setup.py').absolute() ending in docs/../setup.py while resolve() gave setup.py; for the Windows kind a path needs a drive as well as a root, so PureWindowsPath('C:/Users') was absolute and PureWindowsPath('/a/b') and PureWindowsPath('C:') were not, where PurePosixPath('/a/b') was (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: An absolute path starts at the root folder and a relative path is read from the current working directory; is_absolute() tells which, absolute() puts the working directory in front without tidying the path, and resolve() also removes .. and follows links.

io.code: (__import__('pathlib').Path('a/b').is_absolute(), __import__('pathlib').PurePosixPath('/a/b').is_absolute(), __import__('pathlib').PureWindowsPath('/a/b').is_absolute())

nodes.label: Dot and dot dot
nodes.body: A single dot is the name of this folder and two dots the name of the parent folder; they are not real folders but special names, and the .\ at the start of a relative path is optional, so .\spam.txt and spam.txt are the same file (Sweigart, 2025); run here Path('./spam.txt') == Path('spam.txt') was True and str of it 'spam.txt', str(Path('a/../b')) kept the two dots as 'a/../b', and from the folder bacon/eggs Path('..').resolve().name was 'bacon' and Path('../..').resolve() was the parent of the parent (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A single dot names this folder and two dots the parent folder; a leading ./ is optional, so Path('./spam.txt') equals Path('spam.txt'), while .. stays in the path text until resolve() removes it.

io.code: (__import__('pathlib').Path('./spam.txt') == __import__('pathlib').Path('spam.txt'), __import__('pathlib').PurePosixPath('a/../b').parts[:3])

nodes.label: Path anatomy
nodes.body: A path breaks into parts that other paths are built from (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Path attributes
nodes.body: For Path('C:/Users/Al/spam.txt') the anchor is 'C:\\', the name 'spam.txt', the stem 'spam', the suffix '.txt' and the drive 'C:', and the parent is another path, WindowsPath('C:/Users/Al'); the attributes are strings except parent (Sweigart, 2025); reproduced with PureWindowsPath; the chapter says that macOS and Linux path objects have no drive attribute, yet PurePosixPath('/home/al/spam.txt') had the anchor '/' and the drive '', an empty string, and archive.tar.gz having the suffix '.gz', the suffixes ['.tar', '.gz'] and the stem 'archive.tar' (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The name of a path is its last part, made of a stem and a suffix (the extension); parent is the path of the folder that holds it, and anchor and drive give the root and, on Windows, the drive letter; all are strings except parent, which is a path.

io.code: (lambda p: (p.name, p.stem, p.suffix, p.drive, p.anchor, repr(p.parents[1])))(__import__('pathlib').PureWindowsPath('C:/Users/Al/spam.txt'))

nodes.label: Path parts
nodes.body: The parts attribute is a tuple of strings, ('C:\\', 'Users', 'Al', 'spam.txt') for the chapter's path, so parts[3] is 'spam.txt' and parts[0:2] is ('C:\\', 'Users'), and the parents attribute, different from parent, is indexed by an integer, parents[0] being C:/Users/Al and parents[2] C:/ for a path C:/Users/Al/Desktop (Sweigart, 2025); run here len(parents) was 3 for that path and parents of the POSIX path '/home/al/spam.txt' ended at '/', the last step following the parents up to the root folder (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: parts is the tuple of the names of a path from the root on, and parents is a sequence of the folders above it, nearest first, ending at the root; parent and parents are two different attributes.

io.code: (lambda p: (p.parts[1:3], str(p.parents[1]), len(p.parents)))(__import__('pathlib').PurePosixPath('/home/al/spam.txt'))

nodes.label: Derived paths
nodes.body: A new path can be made from an existing one without touching any file (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Path derivation
nodes.body: with_suffix('.csv') turned /home/al/reports/spam.txt into /home/al/reports/spam.csv, with_name('eggs.txt') into /home/al/reports/eggs.txt and relative_to('/home/al') into reports/spam.txt, while relative_to('/usr') raised ValueError, and p.parent / (p.stem + '_backup' + p.suffix) gave /home/al/reports/spam_backup.txt; the chapter as read does not present these methods (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: with_suffix(), with_name() and relative_to() build a new path from an existing one without using a disk, and never change the original; relative_to() raises ValueError when the path does not begin with the other one.

io.code: (str(__import__('pathlib').PurePosixPath('/home/al/spam.txt').with_suffix('.csv').parents[1]), str(__import__('pathlib').PurePosixPath('/home/al/spam.txt').relative_to('/home/al')))

nodes.label: Folders
nodes.body: Folders are created, searched and inspected with os, os.path and pathlib (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Creating folders
nodes.body: The chapter creates folders with os.makedirs() and with the mkdir() method (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Making folders
nodes.body: os.makedirs('C:\\delicious\\walnut\\waffles') creates the folder delicious, the folder walnut in it and the folder waffles in that, all the intermediate folders, and Path(r'C:\Users\Al\spam').mkdir() makes one folder, which needs parents=True to create the folders above it (Sweigart, 2025); run here a second os.makedirs() of the same path raised FileExistsError and did not with exist_ok=True, Path('a/b').mkdir() without the folder a raised FileNotFoundError and with parents=True made both, and a second Path('spam').mkdir() raised FileExistsError unless exist_ok=True was given (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: os.makedirs() creates a folder and every missing folder above it, and Path.mkdir() makes one folder unless parents=True is given; both raise FileExistsError for a folder that exists unless exist_ok=True is given.

io.code: (lambda t, P: (lambda d: (lambda r: (t.cleanup(), r)[1])((lambda q: (q.mkdir(parents=True), sorted(x.name for x in d.rglob('*')))[1])(d / 'delicious' / 'walnut' / 'waffles')))(P(t.name)))(__import__('tempfile').TemporaryDirectory(), __import__('pathlib').Path)

nodes.label: Finding files
nodes.body: The chapter finds the files of a folder with glob patterns (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Glob patterns
nodes.body: In a glob pattern * matches any text and ? exactly one character, so '*.txt' matches the names ending in .txt, 'project?.txt' matches project1.txt, project2.txt and projectX.txt and '*' matches all names; glob() on a folder's path gives a generator that list() turns into a list of paths, or a for loop goes through (Sweigart, 2025); run on a folder of eleven files, '*.txt' gave catproject5.txt, project1.txt, project10.txt, project2.txt, projectX.txt and zzz.txt, 'project?.txt' did not match project10.txt, '*project?.*' also matched secret_project7.docx, '[0-9]*' matched 1.png and 22-ap.pdf, '*' included the folder sub, the file notes.TXT matched only with case_sensitive=False on this Linux machine, sorted() was needed because the order is arbitrary, the object returned was a map, not the generator of the chapter's print, and a second list() of it was empty (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: In a glob pattern * matches any run of characters inside one name, ? matches exactly one character and [seq] one character of a set; glob() gives an iterator that can be used once and in no particular order, so sorted() is used to show its paths.

io.code: (lambda t, P: (lambda d: (lambda r: (t.cleanup(), r)[1])(([d.joinpath(n).write_text('x') for n in ('project1.txt', 'project2.txt', 'projectX.txt', 'project10.txt', 'cat.jpg')], [x.name for x in sorted(d.glob('project?.txt'))], [x.name for x in sorted(d.glob('*.txt'))])[1:]))(P(t.name)))(__import__('tempfile').TemporaryDirectory(), __import__('pathlib').Path)

nodes.label: Recursive glob
nodes.body: The chapter's patterns look at one folder; with a ** segment, glob('**/*.txt') and rglob('*.txt') give the same paths from the whole tree below a folder, which gave top.txt, sub/inner.txt and sub/deeper/deep.txt here, while '*/*.txt' gave only sub/inner.txt and a pattern ending in a slash, 'sub/', gave only the folder sub; the chapter as read does not present rglob() (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A ** segment matches any number of nested folders, so rglob('*.txt') and glob('**/*.txt') search the whole tree below a folder, while '*/*.txt' looks exactly one folder down.

nodes.label: File information
nodes.body: A program asks the file system whether a path exists and what it holds (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Path validity
nodes.body: exists() is True if the path exists, is_file() if it exists and is a file, and is_dir() if it exists and is a folder, and all are False for a path that does not exist, so Path('D:/').exists() is False when no flash drive is attached; the older os.path.exists(), isfile() and isdir() act the same and accept Path objects since Python 3.6 (Sweigart, 2025); run here a file gave True, True, False, a folder True, False, True and a missing path False three times, the os.path functions agreeing, and the documentation adds that in Python 3.14 these methods return False instead of raising any OSError, which needs a path whose check is refused and was not run, the session being a superuser (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: exists(), is_file() and is_dir() answer True or False and do not raise for a path that is missing; the functions of os.path with the same names do the same and accept path objects.

io.code: (lambda t, P: (lambda d: (lambda r: (t.cleanup(), r)[1])(((d / 'f.txt').write_text('x'), [(q.exists(), q.is_file(), q.is_dir()) for q in (d, d / 'f.txt', d / 'nothing')])[1]))(P(t.name)))(__import__('tempfile').TemporaryDirectory(), __import__('pathlib').Path)

nodes.label: File stat
nodes.body: stat() returns a stat_result object whose st_size is the size of the file in bytes, which divided by 1024, 1024 ** 2 or 1024 ** 3 gives kilobytes, megabytes or gigabytes, st_mtime the last modified time, st_ctime the creation time on Windows and the time of the last change of the metadata elsewhere, and st_atime the last access, all in seconds since 1 January 1970, which time.asctime(time.localtime(...)) turns into text (Sweigart, 2025); run here a file holding 'Hello, world!' had st_size 13, which is 0.0126953125 KB, the timestamp set to 1712627129 with os.utime() read back as 1712627129.0 and time.asctime(time.gmtime(...)) gave 'Tue Apr  9 01:45:29 2024', five hours after the 'Mon Apr  8 20:45:29 2024' that the chapter prints for the same second in its own time zone; the documentation deprecates st_ctime on Windows since Python 3.12 in favour of st_birthtime, which was not run on Windows (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: stat() returns a stat_result whose st_size is the size in bytes and whose st_mtime is the time of the last change in seconds since 1 January 1970, which the time module turns into a date; timestamps can be set by hand and are not proof.

io.code: (lambda t, P: (lambda d: (lambda r: (t.cleanup(), r)[1])((lambda f: (f.write_text('Hello, world!'), f.stat().st_size, __import__('os').utime(f, (1712627129, 1712627129)), f.stat().st_mtime)[1::2])(d / 'calc.txt')))(P(t.name)))(__import__('tempfile').TemporaryDirectory(), __import__('pathlib').Path)

nodes.label: Text files
nodes.body: Plain text files are read and written whole with pathlib, or opened as file objects (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Whole file methods
nodes.body: The pathlib methods read_text() and write_text() handle a whole text file in one call (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Write and read text
nodes.body: Path('spam.txt').write_text('Hello, world!') creates the file, or overwrites it, and returns 13, the number of characters written, and read_text() returns 'Hello, world!' (Sweigart, 2025); run here write_text('caf\u00e9', encoding='utf-8') returned 4 while the file held 5 bytes, b'caf\xc3\xa9', a second write_text('again') returned 5 and replaced the first content, and the documentation says the file is opened and closed by each call (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: write_text() creates or overwrites a file with a string and returns the number of characters written, which is not the number of bytes; read_text() opens, reads and closes the file and returns its contents as one string.

io.code: (lambda t, P: (lambda d: (lambda r: (t.cleanup(), r)[1])((lambda f: (f.write_text('caf\u00e9'*2, encoding='utf-8'), f.stat().st_size, ascii(f.read_text(encoding='utf-8'))))(d / 'spam.txt')))(P(t.name)))(__import__('tempfile').TemporaryDirectory(), __import__('pathlib').Path)

steps.expr: (lambda t, P: (lambda d: (lambda r: (t.cleanup(), r)[1])((lambda f: (f.write_text('café' * 2, encoding='utf-8'), f.stat().st_size, ascii(f.read_text(encoding='utf-8'))))(d / 'spam.txt')))(P(t.name)))(__import__('tempfile').TemporaryDirectory(), __import__('pathlib').Path)

nodes.label: Plain versus binary files
nodes.body: Plaintext files hold only basic text characters, with no font, size or colour, and the .txt and .py files are examples; all other files, such as word processing documents, PDFs, images, spreadsheets and programs, are binary files that look like nonsense in Notepad, and the chapter reads and writes only plaintext directly, leaving the binary kinds to modules such as shelve (Sweigart, 2025); run here read_bytes() and write_bytes() returned b'\x00\x01\xff' and 3, open(name, 'rb') returned a BufferedReader whose read() gave bytes, open(name, 'rb', encoding='utf-8') raised ValueError: binary mode doesn't take an encoding argument and writing a string to a file opened with 'wb' raised TypeError: a bytes-like object is required, not 'str' (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A plain text file holds only characters and a binary file anything else; Python reads text as str and binary data as bytes, and read_bytes() and write_bytes() do for bytes what read_text() and write_text() do for text.

io.code: (lambda t, P: (lambda d: (lambda r: (t.cleanup(), r)[1])((lambda f: (f.write_bytes(bytes([0, 1, 255])), f.read_bytes()))(d / 'b.bin')))(P(t.name)))(__import__('tempfile').TemporaryDirectory(), __import__('pathlib').Path)

nodes.label: Opened files
nodes.body: open() returns a file object that is read, written and closed (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Open and modes
nodes.body: open('hello.txt', encoding='UTF-8') opens in read mode, the default, and 'r' can be given; 'w' overwrites and 'a' appends, both creating a missing file; in the chapter's session bacon_file.write('Hello, world!\n') returned 14 and write('Bacon is not a vegetable.') returned 25, and reading the file back printed the two lines (Sweigart, 2025); run here these values were 14 and 25 and the content read as printed, opening with 'w' emptied the file at once, 'a' created fresh.txt, writing to a file opened for reading raised io.UnsupportedOperation: not writable and reading one opened for writing raised io.UnsupportedOperation: not readable, a missing file raised FileNotFoundError, 'x' on an existing file raised FileExistsError and on a new one created it, and 'r+' read 'made' then wrote, the class being a kind of OSError; the chapter's practice question names three modes, 'r', 'w' and 'a' (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: open() returns a file object; mode 'r' reads and is the default, 'w' writes after emptying the file, 'a' appends, 'x' creates a file and fails with FileExistsError if it exists, and 'w', 'a' and 'x' create a missing file; a file opened for reading cannot be written.

nodes.label: Read methods
nodes.body: read() returns the contents of the file as one string and readlines() a list of strings, one for each line, in which each string but the last ends in a newline (Sweigart, 2025); run on the chapter's sonnet file readlines() returned the four strings printed there, a second readlines() returned [] and read() returned '' because the position was at the end, after seek(0) readline() returned the first line with its newline, read(5) 'I all' and read(3) ' al', read() after seek(0) had 171 characters, and a readline() loop counted 4 lines and then returned '' (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: read() returns the rest of the file as one string, readlines() returns the remaining lines as a list in which each line keeps its newline, and readline() returns one line; a file object remembers its position, so a second read() returns an empty string until seek(0).

nodes.label: Line iteration
nodes.body: The chapter reads a file whole with read() or readlines(), and a file object can also be looped over one line at a time, each line keeping its newline, which never holds more than one line in memory; run on the sonnet file the loop gave the lines 'When, in dis', 'I all alone ', 'And trouble ' and 'And look upo' cut to twelve characters, and the last line had no newline because the file does not end with one; the chapter as read does not present it (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A file object is iterated one line at a time without loading the whole file, which is the economical way to go through a large text file; the last line has no newline when the file does not end with one.

nodes.label: Write method
nodes.body:
write() writes a string and returns the number of characters, including the newline, and unlike print() it does not add a newline, so the program must add it (Sweigart, 2025); run here write('a') followed by write('b') and print('c', file=f) gave the file 'abc
', write(42) raised TypeError: write() argument must be str, not int, and writelines(['x
', 'y
']) wrote two lines (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: write() puts exactly the string it is given into the file and returns the number of characters; unlike print() it adds no newline, and a value that is not a string raises TypeError, while print(text, file=f) and writelines() are the alternatives.

io.code: (lambda f: (f.write('ab'*2), f.write('c'), print('d', file=f), f.getvalue()))(__import__('io').StringIO())

nodes.label: Close method
nodes.body: Every file opened with open() needs close() called on it, which the chapter asks for before a file is opened again (Sweigart, 2025); run here a file opened for writing had closed False, write('data') returned 4, another reader of the same file saw '' until close() was called and then 'data', and a write to the closed file raised ValueError: I/O operation on closed file; the tutorial warns that a write without with or close() might not be completely written to the disk even if the program exits successfully (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: close() writes out what is still buffered and releases the file for other programs; data written with write() may not be on the disk until then, and any later use of the closed file raises ValueError.

nodes.label: Text encoding
nodes.body: The encoding and line-ending arguments decide how characters become bytes in a file (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Encoding argument
nodes.body: The encoding argument names the encoding used to convert bytes to a text string; the chapter says it is almost always 'utf-8', the default on macOS and Linux, that Windows defaults to 'cp1252', and that it is a good habit to pass encoding='utf-8' to open() in plaintext modes (Sweigart, 2025); the documentation says the default is platform dependent, whatever locale.getencoding() returns, and recommends UTF-8; run here the bytes b'caf\xc3\xa9' read as 'caf\xe9' with utf-8, as 'caf\xc3\xa9' with latin-1 and cp1252, raised UnicodeDecodeError: 'ascii' codec can't decode byte 0xc3 in position 3: ordinal not in range(128) with ascii, writing it with ascii raised UnicodeEncodeError, and an open() without the argument gave the locale's encoding; with -X warn_default_encoding a call of open() without encoding drew an EncodingWarning and a call with it drew none, and Python 3.15 will make UTF-8 mode the default, which is not so in 3.14.4 (Python Software Foundation, 2026) (Inada, 2019) (Inada, 2022).
nodes.definition: encoding names how the stored bytes become characters; without it Python 3.14.4 uses the encoding of the machine's locale, so text with non-English letters can fail or turn into nonsense on a machine where that is not UTF-8, which is why UTF-8 is written out, and Python 3.15 will make UTF-8 the default.

nodes.body:
In text mode Python reads the line endings 
,  and 
 as 
 and, when writing, turns 
 into the line ending of the system, and the newline argument changes this; the chapter as read does not present the newline argument (Sweigart, 2025); the tutorial warns that the translation corrupts binary data like JPEG or EXE files, and run here write_text('a
b', newline='
') left the bytes b'a
b', read_text() gave 'a
b' and read_text(newline='') 'a
b', and open(..., newline='') wrote b'a
b

nodes.definition: In text mode Python turns a newline into the line ending of the system when writing and any line ending into a newline when reading; the newline argument changes this, and binary mode never translates.

nodes.label: Decoding errors
nodes.body: The errors argument chooses what happens to bytes that cannot be decoded: the default 'strict' raises, 'replace' inserts U+FFFD, 'ignore' drops them and 'surrogateescape' keeps them so that they can be written back; run here open of b'caf\xc3\xa9' with encoding='ascii', errors='replace' read 'caf\ufffd\ufffd'; the chapter as read does not present the errors argument (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Bytes that the encoding cannot decode raise UnicodeDecodeError, and the errors argument chooses another handling, such as 'replace', which puts the character U+FFFD in their place; writing a character the encoding lacks raises UnicodeEncodeError.

io.code: ascii(b'caf\xc3\xa9'.decode('ascii', errors='replace'))

nodes.label: Automatic closing
nodes.body: The with statement closes a file on every way out of a block (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: With statement
nodes.body: A with statement creates a context manager and runs its block, closing the file when execution leaves the block by a return statement, an unhandled exception or otherwise, so the code with open('data.txt', 'w', encoding='UTF-8') as file_obj: needs no close() (Sweigart, 2025); the reference says __exit__ is always called once __enter__ has returned, and run here a file was closed after a block that ended, after one that raised RuntimeError, and after a function that returned from inside the block, the file object having both __enter__ and __exit__ (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A with statement runs its block and then closes the file however the block is left, by reaching its end, by return or by an exception; it works because a file object is a context manager, with __enter__ and __exit__ methods.

io.code: (lambda f: (f.__enter__() is f, f.__exit__(None, None, None), f.closed))(__import__('tempfile').TemporaryFile('w+', encoding='utf-8'))

nodes.label: Closed file error
nodes.body: After the block of a with statement, or after close(), the file object cannot be used: a read or write raises ValueError: I/O operation on closed file, and the attribute closed is True; the chapter as read does not show the error (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Reading or writing a file object that is closed raises ValueError: I/O operation on closed file, and the closed attribute of the object is True once a with block has ended.

nodes.label: Saved data
nodes.body: Variables can outlive the program by being saved to a file (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Shelves
nodes.body: The shelve module saves the values of variables in a binary shelf file and brings them back in a later run (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Shelve open
nodes.body: shelve.open('mydata') returns a shelf value, to which shelf_file['cats'] = ['Zophie', 'Pooka', 'Simon'] stores a list under a key, like a dictionary, and close() ends the use; reopening gives the list again, and type(shelf_file) is <class 'shelve.DbfilenameShelf'> (Sweigart, 2025); run here all of this held, and the folder held the single file mydata; the documentation names the context-manager form with shelve.open('spam') as db and says not to rely on a shelf being closed automatically (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: shelve.open() opens, and creates if needed, a persistent dictionary kept in a file, open for reading and writing at once; it must be closed, or used in a with statement, for everything to be written. In the page, whose Python has no dbm module, the example opens the shelf with shelve.Shelf over an in-memory dictionary, the class that shelve.open() builds on; shelve.open() itself was run under Python 3.14.4 in the Code Lab data.

nodes.label: Shelf as dictionary

In the page, whose Python has no dbm module, the example opens the shelf with shelve.Shelf over an in-memory dictionary, the class that shelve.open() builds on; shelve.open() itself was run under Python 3.14.4 in the Code Lab data.

nodes.label: Shelf writeback
nodes.body: The chapter as read stores values but does not show changing one: run here a shelf holding ['Zophie'] still held ['Zophie'] after shelf['cats'].append('Pooka') was called on a reopened shelf, held ['Zophie', 'Pooka'] when the list was assigned back to the key, and gained 'Simon' in the same way when the shelf was opened with writeback=True; the documentation explains that a shelf cannot know when a mutable entry is modified, and that writeback=True caches every entry accessed and can use much memory and make closing slow (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A shelf cannot see a list that is changed in place, so the change is lost unless the value is assigned back to its key or the shelf is opened with writeback=True, which keeps a cache of the values read and writes it on closing, at a cost in memory and time. In the page, whose Python has no dbm module, the example opens the shelf with shelve.Shelf over an in-memory dictionary, the class that shelve.open() builds on; shelve.open() itself was run under Python 3.14.4 in the Code Lab data.

nodes.label: Shelf backend
nodes.body: The chapter says that after the first shelf the folder holds mydata.bak, mydata.dat and mydata.dir on Windows, a single mydata.db on macOS and a single mydata on Linux, and that the format is not important (Sweigart, 2025); the documentation says that the files depend on the dbm backend, that a new database uses the first of dbm.sqlite3, dbm.gnu, dbm.ndbm and dbm.dumb that can be imported, and that an extension may be added to the filename (Python Software Foundation, 2026); run here the new shelf was made by dbm.sqlite3 as the single file mydata, which sqlite3 could open and whichdb() named, dbm.dumb made dumbdata.bak, dumbdata.dat and dumbdata.dir, which is the Windows list of the chapter, and the lists of Windows and macOS themselves were not run.
nodes.definition: A shelf is built on the dbm package, which uses the first available backend for a new file: in Python 3.14.4 that is dbm.sqlite3, which makes one file named as in the call, while dbm.dumb makes .dat, .dir and .bak files; the file lists the chapter gives for Windows and macOS were not run. This concept has no example in the page: the Python of the page has no dbm module, so the backends were run only under Python 3.14.4 (Code Lab data).

nodes.label: Shelf security
nodes.body: The chapter says to use shelve to save data from Python programs (Sweigart, 2025); the documentation adds that, because shelve is backed by pickle, it is insecure to load a shelf from an untrusted source, since loading can execute arbitrary code, that concurrent reading and writing by two programs is not supported, that values should be fairly small, and that on macOS dbm.ndbm can silently corrupt the file on updates; the warning was read and was not demonstrated, since that would run hostile code (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The values in a shelf are pickled, so loading a shelf from an untrusted source can run arbitrary code, and two programs must not write to one shelf at the same time; a shelf is for a program's own data.

nodes.label: Plain alternative
nodes.body: Plain data can be saved in a format that is not tied to Python (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Json saving
nodes.body: The chapter as read saves data with shelve, and the tutorial presents json for lists and dictionaries: json.dump(x, f) writes and json.load(f) reads, the file must be UTF-8, and only simple types are handled without extra effort; run here json.dumps of a dictionary with a list, an integer and a tuple gave '{'cats': ['Zophie', 'Pooka', 'Simon'], 'count': 3, 'pair': [1, 2], '5': 'five'}', reading it back gave a dictionary that was not equal to the original because the tuple had become a list and the key 5 the string '5', and json.dump with indent=1 and json.load round-tripped a small dictionary (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: JSON writes plain data, dictionaries, lists, strings, numbers, true, false and null, as readable UTF-8 text that other programs and languages can read, so it suits data that is shared or inspected; tuples come back as lists and keys as strings.

nodes.body: The chapter's one project and its two practice programs put the file functions to use (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Quiz program
nodes.body: Project 4 writes 35 different quizzes and their answer keys to text files (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Quiz data
nodes.body: Step 1 imports random, keeps the 50 states and capitals in the dictionary capitals and starts a for loop over range(35) that will make the quiz files (Sweigart, 2025); in the listing as printed the key 'West Virginia' is broken over two lines, and run as a literal newline inside the quotes the compile failed with SyntaxError: unterminated string literal (detected at line 1), while the joined key compiled, the dictionary having 50 keys and 50 different capitals (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

resources.title: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd edition: Chapter 10, Reading and Writing Files
resources.why: The course textbook's own chapter, free online: filepaths, reading and writing text files, shelve and the quiz project.

resources.title: pathlib — Object-oriented filesystem paths
resources.why: Every Path attribute and method of the chapter and more: parts, glob patterns, mkdir, read_text and the 3.14 change to exists().

resources.title: Built-in Functions (open)
resources.why: The full account of open(): every mode, the encoding, errors and newline arguments and the file object types it returns.

resources.title: io — Core tools for working with streams
resources.why: Why the default encoding is the locale's, the advice to write encoding out and the opt-in EncodingWarning.

resources.title: 7. Input and Output
resources.why: The tutorial on reading and writing files: methods of file objects, with, and saving structured data with json.

resources.title: os — Miscellaneous operating system interfaces
resources.why: makedirs, chdir, getcwd and the fields of a stat result, including the change to st_ctime on Windows.

resources.title: shelve — Python object persistence
resources.why: How a shelf works, the writeback argument, the restrictions and the security warning about pickled values.

resources.title: dbm — Interfaces to Unix “databases”
resources.why: Which backend a new database uses and what files dbm.sqlite3 and dbm.dumb make.

resources.title: json — JSON encoder and decoder
resources.why: The format to use for plain data that other programs read, and how Python types map to JSON.

resources.title: 8. Compound statements
resources.why: The exact steps of the with statement, which guarantee that __exit__ is called.

resources.title: PEP 686 – Make UTF-8 mode default
resources.why: Why Python 3.15 makes UTF-8 the default encoding of open().

resources.title: PEP 597 – Add optional EncodingWarning
resources.why: The warning that finds every open() call that leaves the encoding out.

resources.title: PEP 428 – The pathlib module – object-oriented filesystem paths
resources.why: The design of pathlib: pure paths and concrete paths.

resources.title: PEP 519 – Adding a file system path protocol
resources.why: How path objects can be given to open() and to os functions that used to need strings.
